rv.q: There’s Ruby, her daughter: thirtysomething, gorgeous and sensuous, who knows her worth, knows how to use it, and who is desperate to make something of herself. There’s Diamond, the stranger who walks into the club: a man worn sharp and hard through pressure, he claims to be Pearl’s estranged son and wants what he feels is owed to him.

There are contested memories with gentle shocks and apologies. It is beautifully done through their exchanges on the beach. Writer Tim Foley has won several awards for past works (including the Bruntwood prize) and it is clear, from the love and lyricism in this script, that he is a striking talent.
Plot and emotion are dialled up to 11 but don't shake you as they might.
This riveting tale is a promising start for Laird as a playwright.

cn.t: Laird's ambitious debut set in 1950s Trinidad impresses with its textured atmosphere and vivid sense of place, though the execution proves uneven. Critics praise the rich cultural detail and strong characterization.
